column5: The Old Kingdom was an important period of Egyptian state organization and pyramid building. Its approximate dates form the first Egyptian kingdom ribbon. Period boundaries in ancient chronology are estimates, rather than exact dates shared by every historian.

The Middle Kingdom represents a later phase of Egyptian political and cultural history. Its ribbon follows the Old Kingdom with an intervening gap. The dates use the University College London chronology and are approximate.

The New Kingdom was a period of Egyptian expansion and extensive royal building. Its ribbon follows the Middle Kingdom. The approximate beginning and ending dates follow the University College London chronology.
Sumerian cities in southern Mesopotamia supported administrators, craft workers and exchange networks. This is a selected urban period, not a claim that every Sumerian city began or ended together.

The mature Indus period included large urban settlements in South Asia. Excavated brick buildings, streets and drains document sophisticated urban planning. This period is represented separately from later Indian dynasties.
The Parthian Empire ruled extensive territories in Iran and neighboring regions. Its chronology crosses the BCE and CE boundary. Its art reflects contacts across the ancient world.
The Sasanian Empire succeeded Parthian rule in Iran. Its courts and workshops produced distinctive architecture, metalwork and other arts. The ribbon ends in 651 CE.
This ribbon uses the conventional dates for imperial rule in the western Roman world. The eastern empire continued after 476 CE, so its history is shown in a separate ribbon.

Constantinople became an imperial capital in 330 CE. The eastern Roman state, often called the Byzantine Empire, continued until the Ottoman conquest of the city in 1453. This selected range begins with the capital rather than the first existence of Rome.

Qin unified the rival states in 221 BCE and established an imperial dynasty. Its short duration contrasts with the longer Han dynasty that followed. Click the separate unification figure for the turning-point story.

The Han dynasty followed Qin and lasted across the BCE and CE boundary. This long period is important to the history of Chinese government, material culture and exchange. The ribbon represents the broad dynastic range.
The Tang dynasty is a selected period in Chinese history. Its ribbon can be compared with the Islamic-world and eastern Roman chronologies. A dynastic range describes a period, rather than one event.
The Song dynasty follows the Tang in this selected chronology. The intervening gap represents periods omitted from this demo. The dynastic range includes both Northern and Southern Song.
The Ming dynasty belongs to the later Chinese chronology. Its ribbon overlaps the Ottoman and Mughal periods, allowing viewers to compare regions at the same time.

The Qing dynasty ruled China from 1644 until the imperial transition of 1911–1912. Court patronage supported architecture, painting and other arts. This timeline uses 1912 as its ending date, following the Smithsonian exhibition chronology.
The Classic period saw the flourishing of Maya cities and monumental inscriptions in parts of Mexico and Central America. Maya communities and history continued after this period.

The Ottoman Empire developed over several centuries and extended across parts of Europe, Asia and Africa. Its territory and institutions changed substantially over time. The sultanate ended in 1922. The ribbon now extends to that date rather than stopping at the former 1900 chart boundary.
The Mughal dynasty ruled in India from 1526 to 1858. Court patronage supported architecture, painting and luxury arts. The chart also includes a separate story for the beginning of Mughal rule.
The Classical period is a selected phase of ancient Greek history. Sculpture, architecture and other material evidence document its cultural life. Greek history extends before and after this range.

The Abbasid period includes major developments in urban life and the arts. Baghdad and Samarra were important centers. Political control changed during this long range; it should not be read as uninterrupted direct rule everywhere.

Writing developed in southern Mesopotamia around 3200 BCE. Early records helped administrators keep accounts. Cuneiform later served several languages and a much wider range of purposes. This is an approximate development date.

A surviving inscribed monument records laws associated with Hammurabi, king of Babylon. He ruled from 1792 to 1750 BCE. The marker near the end of his reign is approximate and does not claim to date every law precisely.

Johannes Gutenberg developed a system of movable metal type and printing in Europe around 1450. Printing and movable type had earlier histories in East Asia. This marker identifies a European development, rather than the first printing anywhere.

James Watt patented his separate condenser in 1769. Separating condensation from the working cylinder improved steam-engine efficiency. Steam engines existed before Watt; this event marks an important improvement.

The Stockton and Darlington Railway opened in 1825. Its opening is an important milestone in the development of rail transport. The railway combined several operating practices rather than immediately resembling a modern passenger network.

The year 1839 is a landmark in the public emergence of photographic processes. Photography developed through the work of several experimenters and continued to change during the nineteenth century. This marker introduces that broader technological history.
Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859. The book presented his explanation of evolution by natural selection and became a major work in the history of biology.

President Abraham Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863. It declared freedom for enslaved people in areas in rebellion against the United States. Its scope was limited; it did not immediately abolish slavery throughout the country.

Alexander Graham Bell received a telephone patent on March 7, 1876. His telephone experiments were part of a wider history of electrical communication. The date marks this patent, rather than every stage of the invention.

Thomas Edison and his team developed a practical incandescent lamp in 1879. Their work formed part of the development of electric lighting systems. Other inventors also contributed to the history of electric light.

Phoenician coastal cities developed extensive maritime trading networks. Merchants carried goods between Mediterranean ports. By the late eighth century BCE, Phoenicians and Greeks had established trading posts around the Mediterranean. The marker at 1000 BCE introduces a broad period; it does not date the beginning of all Phoenician trade.

column4: Ninth–seventh centuries BCE · selected marker 883 BCE
column5: Nimrud became a major royal center under Ashurnasirpal II, who ruled from 883 to 859 BCE. Palace architecture and surviving inscriptions document Assyrian government and material culture. The illustration is a contextual reconstruction of a city and its officials.

Surviving Neo-Babylonian records document accounts, property and obligations. Babylon remained a major urban center. Persian forces under Cyrus conquered the city in 539 BCE. The selected range follows the dating used for the Metropolitan Museum’s Neo-Babylonian tablets.

The Achaemenid Persian Empire extended across large parts of the ancient Near East. Its capitals, monuments and material culture document a complex imperial world. The period ends with Alexander’s conquests. The illustration evokes Persian court architecture rather than a single precisely dated gathering.

Greek communities of the Archaic period produced distinctive pottery, sculpture and metalwork. Cities and maritime contacts connected parts of the Mediterranean. The market illustration is a contextual reconstruction, not a claim that all Greek city-states were founded in 700 BCE.

The Shang dynasty is the earliest archaeologically documented dynasty in Chinese history. Bronze vessels and excavated remains reveal specialized production and organized settlements. The marker introduces the broad dynastic period; it does not date the invention of bronze metallurgy.

The Zhou dynasty followed the Shang. Its history includes Western and Eastern Zhou periods, with changing political authority. Bronze artifacts and settlements document material culture over this long range. The chart uses a broad dynasty range rather than one continuous level of central control.

column4: First–eighth centuries CE · selected first-century marker
column5: Aksum was an African trading empire connected through Adulis to Red Sea commerce between African, Arabian and Mediterranean communities. Its rulers built monumental urban centers in present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea. Granite stelae, tombs and palace remains record its wealth and architecture. King Ezana adopted Christianity around 330 CE; coin designs changed to reflect this transition. Greek inscriptions on gold coins served international trade, while Ge’ez appeared in local circulation. Economic and political problems contributed to decline, but Aksum’s architectural influence and historical importance continued.

The Gupta period is an important phase of South Asian art and architecture. Surviving objects and buildings document skilled production. This illustration presents craftspeople and scholars as a contextual reconstruction, rather than portraying particular named individuals.

The Mauryan dynasty united a large South Asian empire around 321–185 BCE. Chandragupta Maurya expanded control from Bengal toward Afghanistan; Kautilya, also called Chanakya, is associated with his government. Bindusara extended Mauryan power into central and southern India. Ashoka supported Buddhism and placed edicts on rocks and stone pillars, making royal policies visible across the empire. Pataliputra was the capital. These developments show how conquest, administration, public inscriptions and religious patronage shaped a major ancient state.

Towns of the Low Countries developed important textile industries during the medieval period. Production and exchange connected urban communities. The marker at 1100 CE introduces the wider period covered by the source; it is not the founding date of a single market.

column4: Fifteenth century CE · selected cultural context
column5: Fifteenth-century Italian workshops produced paintings, sculptures and portraits for varied patrons. The Renaissance portrait tradition provides evidence of changing artistic practices. The marker at 1400 CE introduces the century rather than one workshop’s founding.

Akkadian rulers brought rival Sumerian cities under imperial control through conquest. Sargon led campaigns across southern Mesopotamia; his sons Rimush and Manishtushu consolidated the dynasty. Under Naram-Sin, military expansion reached farther north and east. Royal art and finely carved cylinder seals expressed the empire’s power. Later rulers faced struggles over succession, and southern cities recovered independence as Akkadian territory contracted.

Hattusha became the Hittite capital around 1650 BCE. From central Anatolia, rulers including Hattushili I and Murshili I led campaigns toward Syria and Mesopotamia. Later kings fortified the capital and established royal centers such as Carchemish. Rivalry with Egypt involved warfare around Kadesh and later peace negotiations. Assyrian attacks and other pressures reduced Hittite territory. Around 1200 BCE the capital was destroyed and imperial control collapsed; the causes are still debated. Hittite cultural traditions continued in northern Syria.

Ancient Ghana was a West African polity in the western Sahel, distinct from the modern country of Ghana. The Metropolitan Museum uses an approximate 300–1200 CE range. Regional trade networks connected Sahelian communities to wider exchange. Archaeological remains, oral accounts and written records offer different perspectives on political authority. Ghana belongs to a sequence of influential West African states, followed by Mali and Songhay.

Mali developed in West Africa around 1230–1600 CE. Oral traditions describe its founder Sunjata, but historical reconstruction also uses archaeology and written records. The empire belonged to trans-Saharan networks that linked regional production and exchange to distant markets. Civic and religious buildings in cities such as Timbuktu and Jenne reflect the importance of urban communities. Mali’s political history formed part of a changing Sahelian landscape that included Ghana before it and Songhay afterward.

The Songhay Empire is represented here by the Metropolitan Museum’s approximate range of 1464–1591 CE. It was one of the influential states of the western Sahel. Gao and other Niger River cities were part of a regional landscape of trade, civic construction and cultural production. Its history should be read alongside the rise and decline of Mali, rather than treating West Africa as a single unchanged kingdom. Oral narratives, written accounts and material remains provide complementary evidence.

The Angkor period is conventionally displayed as 802–1431 CE. Jayavarman II is associated with the beginnings of Khmer imperial power. Angkor developed into a major center of monumental construction. In the early twelfth century, Suryavarman II commissioned Angkor Wat as his state temple and mausoleum. The buildings provide evidence of royal patronage, skilled work and religious life. Later changes in royal building and political conditions contributed to a gradual transformation; the end date is a timeline convention, not the disappearance of Khmer people.

The Aztec Empire was an alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan, with the Mexica of Tenochtitlan dominant. Its selected political range is 1428–1521 CE. Tribute from conquered regions helped support the capital. Tenochtitlan contained markets, canals, causeways and aqueducts, while craftspeople and farmers supplied urban life. In 1521 the city fell during the Spanish-led conquest. Indigenous communities and cultures continued afterward; the political end of the empire did not mean the end of its peoples.

The Metropolitan Museum dates the Inca state’s major imperial phase to 1438–1532 CE. Cuzco was the center of Tawantinsuyu, the empire of four parts. Military expansion brought territories from northern Ecuador to central Chile under Inca rule. In the 1520s a struggle over succession weakened the state. Spanish invaders arrived during this crisis. The 1532 boundary marks the beginning of the conquest period in this chronology; resistance and Indigenous communities continued beyond it.

Tokugawa Ieyasu was appointed shogun in 1603, formally establishing the military regime. Edo, now Tokyo, became its government center. The shogunate controlled regional lords through administrative obligations and alternating residence in Edo. A long period of relative stability supported urban growth. Merchants and artisans became important patrons of woodblock prints, kabuki and other arts. The political range begins in 1603; some museum art chronologies begin the Edo period in 1615. The regime ended in 1868.

Under Hattushili I, Hattusha became the Hittite capital around 1650 BCE. Defensive walls and gateways strengthened the city. The capital provided a base for military expansion toward Syria. This entry separates the establishment of the capital from the entire Hittite period.

In August 1521 Tenochtitlan fell during the Spanish-led conquest. The devastated city was subsequently demolished and rebuilt as Mexico City, capital of the Viceroyalty of New Spain. This marked a political transformation while Indigenous people and communities continued.

column1: Spanish conquest period begins in the Andes
column5: The Metropolitan Museum’s chronology begins the Andean conquest period in 1532, following the Inca state’s 1438–1532 imperial phase. A struggle over succession had weakened the empire before Spanish invaders arrived. The conquest unfolded over time; this date does not mean that all resistance ended immediately.

In 1603 the emperor appointed Tokugawa Ieyasu shogun. This formally established the Tokugawa regime, with Edo as the seat of government. The appointment was a political landmark following prolonged warfare, distinct from the later cultural flourishing of the Edo period.

The Wright brothers made controlled, powered flights at Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina, on 17 December 1903. Their aircraft combined propulsion with a system for controlling flight. This milestone helped open the age of powered aviation.

The First World War began in 1914 and involved powers and people across several continents. Industrial warfare, mobilization and mass casualties transformed societies. Fighting ended with the armistice of November 1918, followed by peace settlements.

The Second World War is conventionally dated 1939–1945, although war in Asia had earlier beginnings. It was a global conflict that devastated civilian populations and included the Holocaust. The war ended in 1945 and reshaped international politics.

The United Nations came into existence on 24 October 1945 after its Charter was ratified. Its founding followed the destruction of the Second World War. The organization provided a framework for international cooperation, peace and security.

Apollo 11 landed on the Moon on 20 July 1969. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin explored the lunar surface while Michael Collins orbited above. The mission marked the first human landing on another world.

CERN placed World Wide Web software in the public domain on 30 April 1993. Making the software freely available helped the Web spread. The Web is a service built on the Internet, rather than the invention of the Internet itself.

The international Human Genome Project announced completion in April 2003. It produced a foundational reference sequence for studying human DNA. This milestone did not mean that every gap in human genome sequencing had been resolved.

On 11 March 2020 the World Health Organization characterized COVID-19 as a pandemic. This was a milestone in the international public-health response, not the date when infections first began. The pandemic affected health, daily life and economies worldwide.

On 11 September 2001, al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked four passenger aircraft in attacks on the United States. Two struck the World Trade Center, one struck the Pentagon, and one crashed in Pennsylvania after passengers and crew resisted. The attacks profoundly affected security policy and international relations.

Ghana became independent from British colonial rule on 6 March 1957. Its independence was an important milestone in the wider wave of African decolonization. The modern country of Ghana is distinct from the medieval Ghana / Wagadu Empire shown earlier on the timeline.

The financial crisis of 2007–2009 intensified in 2008. Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy on 15 September, amid turmoil at major financial institutions. The crisis spread through international financial markets and contributed to severe economic contraction.

The United States Civil Rights Act became law on 2 July 1964. It prohibited discrimination in public accommodations and addressed employment discrimination, among other provisions. The law was a major achievement of the civil rights movement, rather than the end of the struggle for equal rights.
